title: Contentment (1 Timothy 6:6–12)
hookLine: godliness with contentment is great gain; we brought nothing in
tomorrow: who handed Timothy his faith? two names, one verse.
last: BE NOT WEARY IN WELL DOING.

cards: Money is the root of all evil. It turns up on bumper stickers and in arguments about jobs. It's not what the line says.
In the King James the whole sentence runs: "For the love of money is the root of all evil." The words the love of fell off the front, and they change everything. And the line doesn't stand alone.
It sits in a short passage in a letter to Timothy, a young church leader, about what counts as gain. It starts somewhere softer than money. It starts with enough.

teach.b: Here's the opening: "But godliness with contentment is great gain." Gain is a money word, turned around: yes, faith has a profit, and the profit is enough.

Then the reason, as plain as it gets: "For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out." Empty hands at both ends. "And having food and raiment let us be therewith content."
Raiment is clothing. Food and clothes: that's the line for enough. Then the warning, about those who "will be rich," who set their whole will on it, and the well-known line, whole.

teach.h: THE LOVE OF MONEY, NOT MONEY.
teach.b: Money itself isn't the villain. The love of it is, the grip. Some, the letter says, have "pierced themselves through with many sorrows."
Then, warmly, to Timothy: "But thou, O man of God, flee these things." Run from them, and run toward righteousness, faith, love, patience, meekness. Contentment here isn't giving up.
It's knowing what you're running toward.
And one to tell a friend: in another letter, Paul admits it didn't come naturally. "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content." Learned.
A skill, he says, practiced through plenty and through hunger, not a personality type someone is born with.

how: Some Christians return to 1 Timothy 6:6–8 when making choices about money, and some practice simplicity by giving away what they don't need.

o: saving money so you never run short
giving up on every goal you had

s: the Bible says money is the root of all evil
the King James says the love of money is the root of all evil.
the letter names food and clothes as enough
"having food and raiment let us be therewith content."
contentment here means giving up and wanting nothing
Timothy is told to flee, and run toward righteousness, faith, love, patience.

games.q: your uncle quotes 'money is the root of all evil' to argue your cousin shouldn't take a better-paying job. what does the full verse say?
o: the love of money is the root: the grip, not the paycheck.
money itself is evil, so less is always holier.
the verse is only about Timothy's pay as a church leader.
games.why: the King James says the love of money. the danger is the grip, those who will be rich, not having enough to live on.

practice: Take one sip of water, or one bite of something nearby, and keep it in your mouth a moment longer than usual. Let it be enough, just for this sitting, and notice how little has to be added to make it so.
If a want shows up, a scroll, a list, a someday, let it sit there without arguing, and come back to the taste.

wordCard.voice: Contentment. In First Timothy six: food and clothes, and peace with that, called great gain: the profit nobody can take from you.
